newsitem.title: UK: Protestant Loyalists warn on N.Ireland truce.
newsitem.headline: Protestant Loyalists warn on N.Ireland truce.

text.p: A leading politician linked to pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas warned on Tuesday sectarian bloodshed could return to Northern Ireland if the IRA launched more attacks aimed at ending British rule in the province.

John White, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, said Loyalist guerrilla commanders would "obviously ... re-assess the situation" following Monday's statement by jailed militants that they had lost faith in the province's peace process.
The Protestant Loyalists responded to an Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce in September 1994 with their own ceasefire a month later.
The Catholic-backed IRA ended their truce with bombs in London last February but the Loyalist ceasefire still holds.
White said he understood commanders of outlawed Loyalist groups had not changed their support for their ceasefire but would convey the prisoners' views to rank and file members.
"Obviously they are going to reassess the situation and take on board the views of the prisoners. I think (the truce) can certainly hold at this moment," White told BBC radio.
"However, if there is any reaction from Sinn Fein/IRA, then it makes it much more difficult and there is every likelihood that there could be a return to full-scale conflict."

The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, has been excluded from current multi-party talks on the political future of Northern Ireland, sponsored by the British and Irish Republic governments, until the IRA renews its ceasefire.
Northern Ireland has been spared sectarian bloodshed for two years despite renewed IRA bombings on the British mainland.
Around 1,000 Loyalist and IRA prisoners in the high security Maze Prison are frustrated that Britain did not respond to the 1994 ceasefires by announcing an amnesty.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he could understand the frustration felt by both Loyalist and IRA prisoners but violence was not the answer.
"I certainly would hope that it is not a return to violence because, once violence resumes on their side, then I think the scenario becomes very bleak," he told Irish radio.
White said the Loyalists, who killed hundreds of Catholic nationalists during their campaign to defend British rule, felt Britain had ignored the good faith shown by them in their truce.
"They (prisoners) felt that everything had been done to appease Sinn Fein/IRA and that all concessions that had been granted were towards the nationalist community," White said.

IRA bombs in Britain, and discoveries like a haul of 10 tonnes of explosives and weapons in London last week, have fed Loyalist fears that, despite talk of peace, the IRA remains as determined as ever to use violence to force Britain out of Northern Ireland.

"They felt that there was no way that they (IRA) were going to commit themselves to democratic ways and means, therefore it was inevitable that Loyalist paramilitaries would soon be re-engaged in conflict," White said.
